newsitem.title: TURKEY: IMF sees higher Turk budget deficit, prices -- paper.
newsitem.headline: IMF sees higher Turk budget deficit, prices -- paper.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has said Turkey will likely have a higher budget deficit and inflation next year despite the government's zero-deficit budget proposal for 1997, a Turkish newspaper reported on Friday.

The respected liberal daily Yeni Yuzyil quoted a report, which it said was prepared by a team that visited Turkey in October and presented to the IMF presidency, as saying that Turkey's balanced budget in 1997 would be "a success" if it can be achieved.
But it expressed reservations in almost all targets of the proposed budget, currently being debated in parliament and to be voted on by mid-December.
It also said the inflation rate would soar to 100 percent because the government's plan to extend maturities in domestic borrowing next year was very optimistic.
The government seeks to exend its average domestic borrowing maturity to lower high interest rates which it believes will curb inflation, now running at around 80 percent.

The daily said the report expected a budget deficit of 3,014 trillion lira in 1997, with revenues standing at 5,260 trillion lira, spendings 8,274 trillion lira and investments 590 trillion lira in 1997.

The government's draft budget envisages 5,095 trillion lira in revenues, 6,256 trillion lira in spendings including 525 trillion lira of investments, and 1,161 trillion lira in "other revenues", which the government said would be from the sale of public assets.
But the report predicted Turkey's privatisation revenues at only 358 trillion lira in 1997 because it said the money to be raised through sell-offs could not reach the treasury's coffers before 1998.

It said transfers from the budget to close deficits of the social security system, a major black hole draining state funds, would be 2.8 percent of gross national product in 1997, compared to the government estimate of 2.1 percent.
The IMF believed Turkey's chances of tapping foreign borrowing sources would be slimmer next year in view of a possible downgrading by international credit rating agencies, Yeni Yuzyil said.
That will force the government to finance deficits through domestic borrowings, which in turn would raise rates, shorten maturities and boost inflation, it said.
